recipe.history: The true yam — Dioscorea species, not to be confused with the sweet potato that Americans commonly call a yam — is one of the most important staple crops in the world, cultivated across sub-Saharan Africa, West Africa, the Caribbean, and parts of Asia and Oceania, feeding hundreds of millions of people and carrying enormous cultural and ceremonial significance in the societies that depend upon it. In West Africa, where the majority of the world's yam production occurs, the yam is not merely food — it is identity, ceremony, and calendar. The Igbo people of Nigeria celebrate the New Yam Festival, Iwa Ji or Iri Ji, each August or September to mark the harvest of the first yams of the season, offering the first fruits to ancestors and deities before consuming them, a ceremony that dates back centuries and links the living to those who came before through the ritual of food. The yam was brought to the Americas by enslaved Africans during the Atlantic slave trade — a fact that makes the yam not only a crop but a living cultural continuity, a thread connecting people forcibly removed from their homelands to their culinary and spiritual traditions. In the American South, the cultural vocabulary around yams and sweet potatoes merged and blurred over generations, with orange-fleshed sweet potatoes taking on the name "yam" in American commercial culture. What Americans call candied yams — sweet potatoes glazed with brown sugar, butter, cinnamon, and sometimes marshmallow — is itself a product of this history, a dish rooted in West African culinary tradition and transformed by the American South into something distinctly its own.
recipe.history2: Yams and sweet potatoes entered the American burger imagination through the same broadening of culinary vocabulary that brought roasted beets and caramelized onions onto buns — the understanding, developed gradually through the craft burger movement of the 2000s and 2010s, that a burger can carry any flavor that has sweetness, richness, or contrast to offer. Candied yam as a burger topping takes what is already a deeply pleasurable combination of sweet and savory — the holiday side dish where butter-glazed orange flesh meets brown sugar and spice — and applies it in a format where it works against the mineral richness and fat of beef. The yam aioli brings the same flavor into a spreadable form: roasted sweet potato flesh blended with mayonnaise, spice, and a little acid creates a spread that is simultaneously familiar and unexpected, sweet and creamy in a way that catsup aspires to and never quite achieves. Together, the candied yam topping and yam aioli create a burger that tastes like the best part of a holiday meal condensed into something you can hold with two hands.
recipe.history3_personal: I did not eat candied yams as a child. My family's Thanksgiving table ran to the conventional: turkey, stuffing, green bean casserole, cranberry sauce from a can. It was not until I was invited to Thanksgiving at a friend's house in my late twenties — a house where the cooking was serious and abundant and the table was crowded with three generations of people who had strong feelings about every dish — that I ate candied yams for the first time. They were nothing like I expected: not the pale, marshmallow-covered thing I had imagined from cultural references, but dense and yielding wedges of orange sweet potato, glazed with cane sugar and butter and spiced with cinnamon and a little cayenne, the exterior caramelized to a sticky amber that pulled apart in long strands. I ate four servings before anyone asked if I wanted more. I drove home that night thinking about them and went to the grocery store the following morning to buy sweet potatoes. I have made some version of candied yams every November since, and I have been looking for other contexts to deploy them ever since. The burger was an inevitability. It was always going to happen.
recipe.history4_philosophy: There is a version of this burger that could be made with a well-done patty, and it would be a fine thing — the sweetness of the candied yam and the richness of the aioli would still be present, and the burger would be satisfying in the way that any burger with enough good toppings can be satisfying regardless of what has happened to the patty. But that version would be missing the central element that makes this combination more than the sum of its parts. At medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — the beef patty contributes a deep, iron-rich, fat-lubricated juiciness that is the ideal base for the sweetness of the candied yam. The sweetness needs something savory and mineral to push against; the beef's richness needs something sweet and yielding to provide contrast and relief. They are made for each other at this specific temperature. The yam aioli, spread on the warm toasted bun, needs the warmth of the patty to stay fluid and fragrant. Everything in this burger is calibrated around the assumption of a medium rare patty. Cook it right. There is no other way.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
2 large garnet sweet potatoes or true yams (about 700g total), peeled
1 medium garnet sweet potato (about 200g), roasted whole
4 thick slices sharp orange cheddar cheese
instructions: 1. Roast the aioli sweet potato: Preheat oven to 400°F / 204°C. Pierce the sweet potato for the aioli all over with a fork. Place directly on the oven rack (or on a foil-lined baking sheet to catch drips). Roast 45–55 minutes until completely tender when pierced and caramelized juices are oozing from the skin. Remove and let cool. Once cool enough to handle, scoop the flesh from the skin — you should have about 120g of roasted flesh.

2. Make the yam aioli: Combine roasted sweet potato flesh, mayonnaise, lime juice, smoked paprika, cinnamon, cayenne, garlic powder, salt, and honey in a blender or food processor. Blend until completely smooth. Taste and adjust seasoning — it should be sweet, smoky, and slightly spicy. Refrigerate until needed.

3. Make the candied yam topping: Cut the peeled sweet potatoes into 1/2-inch-thick rounds or half-moon slices. Melt butter in a large skillet over medium heat until foaming. Add sweet potato slices in a single layer (work in batches if needed). Cook 4–5 minutes per side until golden and starting to soften.

4. Add brown sugar, maple syrup, cinnamon, nutmeg, cayenne, salt, orange juice, and orange zest to the pan. Stir gently to coat the sweet potato slices. Reduce heat to medium-low and cook 8–12 minutes more, turning occasionally, until the sweet potatoes are completely tender, deeply caramelized, and coated in a thick, sticky glaze. Remove from heat. Keep warm.
5. Cook the bacon: In a separate skillet over medium heat, cook bacon strips until crisp and rendered. Drain on paper towels. Set aside.

6. Make the buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer with the dough hook. Add warm milk, water, and egg. Mix on low 2 minutes, then medium 4 minutes. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time. Mix on medium-high 6–8 minutes until smooth and elastic. Rise in a covered oiled bowl 1–1.5 hours until doubled.

7. Divide bun dough into 4 portions, shape into tight balls, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, flatten gently. Proof covered 45–60 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F / 190°C for 15–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool completely.

8. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 225g each). Press into round patties 3/4 inch thick and 4 inches across. Press a dimple in the center. Season both sides generously with salt, black pepper, smoked paprika, and cayenne just before cooking.
9. Cook the patties: Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat for 3 minutes until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Place patties in the skillet. Cook undisturbed 3 minutes.

10. Flip once. Place a thick slice of sharp cheddar on each patty. Cook 2–3 more minutes, covering the pan in the last minute to melt the cheese fully. Check internal temperature — target 130–135°F / 54–57°C for medium rare. Remove from heat and rest 3–4 minutes on a wire rack.
11. Rewarm the candied yams gently over medium-low heat if they have cooled, adding a splash of water if the glaze has tightened too much.
12. Toast the buns: Slice buns and spread yam aioli on both cut sides of the top and bottom buns. Toast cut-side down in a lightly buttered skillet over medium heat until golden, 1–2 minutes.

13. Assemble: On the bottom bun over the toasted aioli, add shredded butter lettuce. Place the rested cheddar-topped patty on the lettuce. Lay a strip of crisp bacon over the patty. Arrange 3–4 slices of candied yam over the bacon, spooning any extra glaze from the pan over everything. Add a pinch of flaky salt. Close with the top bun and serve immediately while the yams are still warm and sticky.
